text:
Predicates:
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
Schedules(x) ::: x schedules a meeting with their customers.
GoesToBuilding(x) ::: x will go to the company building today.
HasLunchInBuilding(x) ::: x has lunch in the company building.
HasLunchAtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
WorksRemotely(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
InOtherCountry(x) ::: x is in other countries.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
AppearsInCompany(x) ::: x will appear in the company today.
Premises:
∀x (Employee(x) ∧ Schedules(x) → GoesToBuilding(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will go to the company building today.
∀x (HasLunchInBuilding(x) → Schedules(x)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (Employee(x) → HasLunchInBuilding(x) ⊕ HasLunchAtHome(x)) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
∀x (HasLunchAtHome(x) → WorksRemotely(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
∀x (InOtherCountry(x) → WorksRemotely(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
∀x (Manager(x) → ¬WorksRemotely(x)) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
AppearsInCompany(james) ↔ Manager(james) ::: James will appear in the company today if and only if he is a manager.
Conclusion:
(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountry(james)) → ¬(HasLunchAtHome(james) ∨ WorksRemotely(james)) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then James does not either have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
(HasLunchAtHome(james) ∨ WorksRemotely(james)) → (¬Manager(james) ∧ ¬InOtherCountry(james)) ::: If James either has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor does he work in other countries.
